summary: This informational document describes how TCP, MPTCP, SCTP, UDP and UDP-Lite expose their services to applications and how applications can configure and use these features. It is part of work on a more flexible transport API.

plainLanguage.summary: This document takes five transport protocols and lists what each can do for the program using it. The lists are then put into one common set of names, so an application could ask for what it wants rather than for a particular protocol's way of asking.

subtitle: A catalogue of what TCP, MPTCP, SCTP, UDP and UDP-Lite offer applications, boiled down into protocol-independent transport features.

tldr.problem: Applications that pick a transport protocol have to learn each protocol's own vocabulary of calls and options, so they cannot change transport without rewriting their code.
tldr.mechanism: The document reads the specifications of five transport protocols, recasts what each one offers as a uniform list of primitives and events, and then presents the superset of transport features with a note of which protocols implement each.
tldr.outcome: It is a working document rather than an interface: it publishes the analysis so that a transport services API can be built on top of it, and it asks for no IANA actions.

today: RFC 8303 is an Informational document with no obsoleting or updating RFC recorded against it, so it stands as the published analysis of transport protocol services for the TAPS work. It requires no IANA actions, and the companion document RFC 8304 covers the same analysis for UDP and UDP-Lite.

sections.title: Why Look at Transport Services at All
sections.content:
The document describes how transport protocols offer transport services, such that applications using them are no longer directly tied to a specific protocol. Breaking this strict connection can reduce the effort for an application programmer, yet attain greater transport flexibility by pushing complexity into an underlying transport services system.

The design process began with a survey of the services provided by IETF transport protocols and congestion control mechanisms. This document and its companion complement that survey with an in-depth look at the defined interactions between applications and five unicast transport protocols: TCP, MultiPath TCP, SCTP, UDP and UDP-Lite. It also defines a primitive to enable, disable and configure the LEDBAT unicast congestion control mechanism. For UDP and UDP-Lite, the first step of the protocol analysis, a discussion of the relevant RFC text, is documented separately.

This snapshot in time of the IETF transport protocols is published as an RFC to document the analysis by the authors and the TAPS Working Group, and it generates a set of transport abstractions that can be exported in a TAPS API. It provides the basis for the minimal set of transport services that end systems supporting TAPS should implement.

The list of primitives, events and transport features is strictly based on the parts of protocol specifications that describe what the protocol provides to an application and how the application interacts with it. Transport protocols provide communication between processes on network endpoints, which means they allow multiplexing between the same IP addresses, achieved using port numbers; port multiplexing is therefore assumed to be always provided and is not discussed further. Parts of a protocol that are explicitly optional to implement are not covered, and interactions not directly related to the operation of the protocol are not covered either: for example there are various ways for an application to use socket options to indicate its interest in receiving certain notifications, but for the purpose of identifying primitives, events and transport features, the ability to enable or disable the reception of notifications is irrelevant. The same applies to one-to-many style sockets, which affect the application's programming style rather than how the underlying protocol operates, and to the ability to obtain the unchanged value of a parameter an application has previously set.
sections.plainLanguage: The goal is to let an application say what it needs, such as reliable ordered delivery, and leave the choice of protocol to the system underneath. To do that, the document first works out exactly what each protocol currently offers.

sections.title: The Vocabulary
sections.content:
A Transport Feature is a specific end-to-end feature that the transport layer provides to an application, such as confidentiality, reliable delivery, ordered delivery, or message- versus stream-orientation. A Transport Service is a set of transport features, without an association to any given framing protocol, that provides a complete service to an application. A Transport Protocol is an implementation that provides one or more transport services using a specific framing and header format on the wire. A Transport Protocol Component is an implementation of a transport feature within a protocol. A Transport Service Instance is an arrangement of transport protocols with a selected set of features and configuration parameters that implement a single transport service, for example a protocol stack such as RTP over UDP.

An Application is an entity that uses the transport layer for end-to-end delivery of data across the network, which may also be an upper-layer protocol or a tunnel encapsulation. An Endpoint is an entity that communicates with one or more other endpoints using a transport protocol. A Connection is shared state of two or more endpoints that persists across the messages transmitted between them.

A Primitive is a function call used to communicate locally between an application and a transport endpoint, and is related to one or more transport features. An Event is a primitive invoked by a transport endpoint. A Parameter is a value passed between an application and a transport protocol by a primitive. A Socket is the combination of a destination IP address and a destination port number, and a Transport Address is the combination of an IP address, transport protocol and the port number used by the transport protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The document separates what a protocol is made of from what an application asks of it. A feature is one capability, a service is a complete set of them, and a primitive is the call an application makes to ask for or change one.

sections.title: Pass One: What Each Protocol Actually Offers
sections.content:
The first pass summarises the relevant text of the RFCs describing the protocols, focusing on what each transport protocol provides to the application and how it is used. When presenting primitives, events and parameters, the use of lower- and upper-case characters is made uniform for the sake of readability.

TCP. The initial specification lists several transport primitives for the interaction with the application. Open is either active or passive, to initiate a connection or listen for incoming connections; a passive open call can leave the socket unspecified to accept any incoming connection, and a fully specified passive call can later be made active by calling Send. Optionally a timeout can be specified, after which TCP will abort the connection if data has not been delivered, and the application can control the threshold used to determine the condition for aborting, which may be measured in time units or as a count of retransmissions. For multihomed hosts the local IP address can be provided. The options parameter allows the application to specify IP options such as Source Route, Record Route or Timestamp, and Source Route is the only non-optional IP option in this parameter. Master Key Tuples for authentication can optionally be configured when calling Open. TCP Fast Open allows applications to hand over a message from the active open to the passive open side together with the first message establishment packet, which can be useful for applications sensitive to TCP's connection setup delay; the size of that message cannot be more than TCP's maximum segment size, and the receiving application must be prepared to accept duplicates because the first data written to a socket can be delivered more than once.

MPTCP is an extension to TCP that allows the use of multiple paths for a single data stream, achieved by creating different TCP subflows for each interface and scheduling traffic across them. It must follow the same service model as TCP, namely in-order, reliable and byte-oriented delivery, and a multipath connection should give the application no worse throughput or resilience than a single TCP connection over any one of its paths. A multipath-capable equivalent of TCP must retain some level of backward compatibility with existing TCP APIs, so that existing applications can use the newer transport merely by upgrading the operating systems of the end hosts. The primitives are therefore equivalent to those of TCP, with clarifications and extensions: an application should be able to request to turn MPTCP on or off, and MPTCP must be disabled when the application binds to a specific address; sending and receiving need no changes for the application, since the MPTCP layer takes one input data stream and splits it into subflows with enough control information to reassemble it; an application should be able to restrict MPTCP to a given set of addresses and to obtain information on the pairs of addresses used by the subflows.

SCTP removes a number of TCP limitations that translate directly into transport features visible to an application: it allows preservation of message delimiters, it does not provide in-order or reliable delivery unless the application wants that, and multihoming is supported. UDP and UDP-Lite are covered in a separate document. LEDBAT is a congestion control mechanism rather than a transport protocol, so it has no primitives of its own; it is designed for background bulk-transfer applications to be no more aggressive than standard TCP congestion control and to yield in the presence of competing flows, limiting interference with the network performance of competing flows. It can be used as part of a transport protocol or as part of an application, as long as the data transmission mechanisms can carry timestamps and acknowledge data frequently, and it can be used with TCP, SCTP and DCCP with appropriate extensions, which at the time of writing do not exist, as well as with proprietary application protocols such as those built on UDP for peer-to-peer applications.
sections.plainLanguage: Pass one is the reading stage. For each protocol the document lists the calls an application can make, such as opening a connection or sending a message, and notes the extra knobs that protocol offers. Multihoming is SCTP's headline addition: it keeps message boundaries and lets an application ask for reliable delivery or not.

sections.title: Pass Two: One Set of Names for All of Them
sections.content:
This pass categorises the primitives from pass one by whether they relate to a connection or to data transmission. Primitives are presented following the nomenclature CATEGORY.SUBCATEGORY.PRIMITIVENAME.PROTOCOL. The category can be CONNECTION or DATA; within the CONNECTION category the subcategories are ESTABLISHMENT, AVAILABILITY, MAINTENANCE and TERMINATION, and the DATA category has no subcategory. The protocol name UDP(-Lite) is used when primitives are equivalent for UDP and UDP-Lite, and TCP refers to both TCP and MPTCP. The document presents connection as a general protocol-independent concept, used to refer to TCP connections, identifiable by a unique pair of IP addresses and TCP port numbers, SCTP associations, identifiable by multiple IP address and port number pairs, and UDP and UDP-Lite connections, identifiable by a unique socket pair.

Some minor details are omitted for the sake of generalization. The TCP Send and Receive primitives include an urgent parameter, which controls a mechanism required to implement the synch signal used by telnet, but since new applications should not employ the TCP urgent mechanism, it is excluded. Because LEDBAT is a congestion control mechanism and not a protocol, it is not currently defined when to enable, disable or configure it; it could be a one-time choice upon connection establishment or when listening for incoming connections, and to avoid unnecessarily limiting future implementations it was placed under CONNECTION.MAINTENANCE, with all parameters described in its specification made configurable.

The LEDBAT specification has a number of configurable parameters. TARGET, the queuing delay target at which LEDBAT tries to operate, must be set to 100 ms or less. The allowed_increase parameter, which should be 1 and must be greater than 0, limits the speed at which LEDBAT increases its rate. The gain parameter, which must be set to 1 or less to avoid a faster ramp-up than TCP Reno, determines how quickly the sender responds to changes in queueing delay; implementations may divide it into two parameters, one for increase and a possibly larger one for decrease, called Gain_Inc and Gain_Dec. Base_History is the size of the list of measured base delays and should be 10; this list can be filtered using a Filter function, which is not prescribed, that yields a list of size Current_Filter. The initial and minimum congestion windows, Init_CWND and Min_CWND, should both be 2. The Filter function is not regarded as a parameter because function implementations are not provided as a parameter to any of the transport protocols discussed; all the other parameters are considered tunable and should be exposed, to avoid unnecessarily limiting future implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: Pass two renames everything so that the same category covers all protocols. Calls fall into four buckets: opening a connection, being ready to receive one, adjusting one that is open, and closing it. Data transfer sits outside those buckets.

sections.title: Pass Three: The Full List of Transport Features
sections.content:
This section presents the superset of all transport features in all the protocols discussed, based on the list of primitives in pass two but also on text in pass one, to include transport features that can be configured in one protocol and are static properties in another, congestion control for example. Minor details are omitted for the sake of generalization, and as before UDP(-Lite) represents both UDP and UDP-Lite while TCP refers to both TCP and MPTCP.

The connection-related features are grouped under four headings. ESTABLISHMENT is the active creation of a connection from one transport endpoint to one or more transport endpoints: Connect, provided by TCP, SCTP and UDP(-Lite); specifying which IP options must always be used; requesting multiple streams and limiting the number of inbound streams, both SCTP only; specifying the number of attempts or timeout for the first establishment message; obtaining multiple sockets, which is SCTP only; disabling MPTCP; configuring authentication, which with TCP allows configuration of Master Key Tuples and in SCTP allows specifying which chunk types must always be authenticated; indicating an adaptation layer through an adaptation code point; requesting to negotiate interleaving of user messages; handing over a message to reliably transfer before connection establishment, which TCP provides, or during connection establishment, which SCTP provides; and enabling UDP encapsulation with a specified remote UDP port number.

AVAILABILITY is preparing to receive incoming connection requests: listening on one specified local interface, on N specified local interfaces, which only SCTP offers, or on all local interfaces; obtaining a requested number of streams and limiting the number of inbound streams; specifying which IP options must always be used; disabling MPTCP; configuring authentication; and indicating an adaptation layer.

MAINTENANCE covers adjustments made to an open connection, or notifications about it: changing the timeout for aborting the connection using a retransmit limit or a time value; suggesting a timeout to the peer; disabling the Nagle algorithm; requesting an immediate heartbeat; notification of excessive retransmissions; adding or removing a path, which MPTCP and SCTP offer; setting the primary path and suggesting a primary path to the peer; configuring path switchover; obtaining status as a query or notification; specifying the DSCP field; notification of an ICMP error message arrival; changing authentication parameters and obtaining authentication information; resetting a stream or an association and being notified of it; adding streams; choosing a scheduler to operate between the streams of an association and configuring its priority or weight; specifying the IPv6 flow label; configuring send and receive buffer sizes, message fragmentation, path MTU discovery and the delayed SACK timer; setting the cookie life value and the maximum burst; configuring the size at which messages are broken up for partial delivery; disabling the checksum when sending and disabling the checksum requirement when receiving, both UDP only; specifying checksum coverage used by the sender and the minimum coverage required by the receiver, both UDP-Lite only; specifying the DF field and obtaining the maximum transport-message size that may be sent or received using a non-fragmented IP packet, UDP(-Lite) only; specifying and obtaining the TTL or hop count field, the ECN field and the IP options, UDP(-Lite) only; and enabling and configuring LEDBAT on a protocol that implements it.

TERMINATION is closing a connection gracefully or forcefully, or being informed that it is happening: closing after reliably delivering all remaining data, and aborting without delivering remaining data, both with a notification to the other side, provided by TCP and SCTP; aborting without delivering remaining data and without notifying the other side, provided by UDP(-Lite); and a timeout event when data could not be delivered for too long.

The data-transfer features refer to an existing connection. TCP allows the transfer of data, a single optional user message possibly arriving multiple times, before the connection is fully established, and reliable data transfer entails delay. When sending, the features are: reliably transferring data with congestion control, which TCP provides; reliably transferring a message with congestion control, which SCTP provides; unreliably transferring a message with congestion control, also SCTP; unreliably transferring a message without congestion control, which UDP(-Lite) provides; configurable message reliability and choice of stream or path, both SCTP only; ordered message delivery, which may be slower than unordered, and unordered message delivery, which may be faster, provided by SCTP and UDP(-Lite); requesting that messages not be bundled; specifying a payload protocol identifier; specifying a key identifier to authenticate a message; and requesting that the acknowledgement of a message not be delayed.

When receiving, the features are receiving data with no message delimiting, which TCP provides; receiving a message, which SCTP and UDP-Lite provide; choice of stream to receive from; and information about partial message arrival, where in SCTP partial messages are combined with a stream sequence number so the application can restore the correct order of the data blocks an entire message consists of. The error features are notification of an unsent part of a message, provided by SCTP and UDP(-Lite); notification of an unacknowledged part of a message; notification that the stack has no more user data to send; and notification to a receiver that a partial message delivery has been aborted.
sections.plainLanguage: Pass three is the catalogue: every capability any of the five protocols offers, each tagged with the protocols that provide it. It is the list a future application interface would be built from.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Authentication, confidentiality protection and integrity protection are identified as transport features. These features are generally provided by a protocol or layer on top of the transport protocol; none of the transport protocols considered in the document provides them on its own. They are therefore not considered in the document, with the exception of the native authentication capabilities of TCP and SCTP, for which the security considerations in the TCP Authentication Option and in the authenticated chunks specification for SCTP apply.

Security considerations for the use of UDP and UDP-Lite are provided in the referenced RFCs, and security guidance for application usage is provided in the UDP usage guidelines.
sections.plainLanguage: None of these protocols encrypts or protects data on its own; that is left to a layer above. Only the built-in authentication of TCP and SCTP is discussed here, and it points at the documents that cover it.

items.title: Transport feature
items.text: A specific end-to-end feature the transport layer provides to an application, such as reliable or ordered delivery.

items.title: Transport service
items.text: A set of transport features, with no association to any framing protocol, that gives an application a complete service.

items.title: Transport protocol
items.text: An implementation providing one or more transport services using a specific framing and header format on the wire.

items.title: Transport service instance
items.text: An arrangement of transport protocols with a selected set of features and parameters that implement a single service, such as RTP over UDP.

items.title: Primitive
items.text: A function call used to communicate locally between an application and a transport endpoint.

items.title: Event
items.text: A primitive that is invoked by a transport endpoint rather than by the application.

items.title: Parameter
items.text: A value passed between an application and a transport protocol by a primitive.

viz.caption: What the five protocols offer, as recorded in pass one

cells: Ordered message delivery is available and may be slower than unordered.
Unordered message delivery, which may be faster.
Does not provide in-order or reliable delivery unless the application wants that.
Yes, with a choice of stream and a scheduler between them.
MPTCP uses several paths, but follows the TCP service model.
Present on reliable and unreliable transfer.

viz.caption: The categories used to organise the transport features

items.title: Establishment
items.text: Active creation of a connection from one transport endpoint to one or more transport endpoints.

items.title: Availability
items.text: Preparing to receive incoming connection requests.

items.title: Maintenance
items.text: Adjustments made to an open connection, or notifications about it.

items.title: Termination
items.text: Gracefully or forcefully closing a connection, or being informed about it happening.

items.title: Data send
items.text: Handing a block of data to the transport to transfer, which is a message if the beginning and end can be identified at the receiver.

items.title: Data receive
items.text: Filling a buffer provided by the application with what arrived, again a message if the beginning and end can be identified.
